title: Using sources: quoting, paraphrasing, citing and plagiarism
blurb: Choose between quoting, paraphrasing and summarizing, cite every borrowed idea, and recognize every form of plagiarism.
question: A student copies two sentences from a health website, swaps a few words for synonyms, keeps the original sentence order and adds a citation. Is that an acceptable paraphrase, or is it plagiarism?

teach.h: Three ways to borrow, one rule
teach.body: Formally, a writer can integrate a source as a direct quotation (the exact words), a paraphrase (one passage restated in new words) or a summary (the main ideas, condensed). Each one must be cited. In plain English: whenever the words OR the idea came from someone else, you give them credit. The only material that needs no citation is common knowledge: widely known, undisputed facts such as 'The heart has four chambers.'

teach.caption: Use quotations sparingly, for wording that is powerful or precise.

teach.body: Original (Kim, 2024): "A friendly greeter in the first minutes of a hospital visit can ease anxiety, especially for patients who arrive alone." Quotation: Kim (2024) notes that a greeter "can ease anxiety." Paraphrase: Patients who come by themselves may feel calmer when someone welcomes them at the door (Kim, 2024). Patchwriting (plagiarism): A friendly greeter in the first minutes of a visit can calm worry, mainly for patients arriving alone (Kim, 2024).

children.label: Did you use the exact words?

teach.caption: Every path except common knowledge ends in a citation.

teach.body: Plagiarism is presenting another person's words or ideas as your own. It is not limited to copying whole sentences. It includes copying without quotation marks, a 'paraphrase' that keeps the original wording or sentence structure (patchwriting), leaving out citations, and reusing your own previous work without permission. Adding a citation does not rescue patchwriting: copied wording needs quotation marks, and a paraphrase needs genuinely new words and structure.

head: What happened
Why it is plagiarism
rows: Exact words passed off as yours

teach.caption: Both styles pair in-text citations in the body with a full list of sources at the end.

teach.body: Aaliyah Washington is writing an APA paper on study habits for her prerequisite course. She states that the heart has four chambers with no citation (common knowledge). She quotes a professor's memorable phrase in quotation marks and cites it. She rewrites a journal finding in her own words and sentence structure, then cites it as (Lopez, 2022). At the end, she lists every source in her reference list. She does not reuse last term's essay, because that would need her instructor's permission.

teach.text: The top TEAS trap: 'A paraphrase is in my own words, so it doesn't need a citation.' Wrong: paraphrases and summaries are always cited, because the IDEA still belongs to the source. Second trap: swapping a few synonyms while keeping the original sentence order is patchwriting, which is plagiarism even with a citation.

items: Quotation: exact words in quotation marks, cited; use sparingly.
Paraphrase: one passage in your own words and structure, about the same length, cited.
Summary: main ideas only, much shorter, own words, cited.
Plagiarism covers words or ideas: no quotation marks, patchwriting, missing citations, reused own work.
Common knowledge needs no citation. APA = author-date (nursing); MLA = author-page (humanities).

summary: You can now decide when to quote, paraphrase or summarize, and you know that all three must be cited. You can also recognize every form of plagiarism, including patchwriting and reusing your own work, and identify APA and MLA citation formats.

A.q: Which statement about paraphrasing is correct?
options: A paraphrase in your own words still needs a citation
A paraphrase needs no citation once the wording changes
A paraphrase keeps the original sentence structure intact
A paraphrase condenses a whole article to its main ideas
A.why: A paraphrase restates a specific passage in new words and structure, but the idea still belongs to the source, so it must be cited.

whyNot.1: Changing the words does not change who owns the idea; leaving out the citation is plagiarism.
whyNot.2: Keeping the original structure is patchwriting, a form of plagiarism; a paraphrase uses new structure too.
whyNot.3: Condensing a whole work to its main ideas describes a summary, not a paraphrase.

A.q: Which of the following can a student include in a research paper without a citation?
options: A survey result reported in a nursing journal
The fact that the heart has four chambers
An expert's opinion restated in your own words
A statistic taken from a public health website
A.why: That the heart has four chambers is common knowledge: widely known and undisputed, so it needs no citation.

whyNot.0: A specific survey result comes from one source's research, so it must be cited.
whyNot.2: Restating an opinion in your own words is a paraphrase, and the idea must still be credited.
whyNot.3: A statistic is specific information from a source and needs a citation.

A.q: A nursing instructor requires the citation style most often used in nursing and the social sciences. Which style is it, and what in-text system does it use?
options: MLA, which uses author-page citations
MLA, which uses author-date citations
APA, which uses author-page citations
APA, which uses author-date citations
A.why: APA is common in nursing and the social sciences and uses author-date in-text citations, such as (Kim, 2024).

whyNot.0: MLA does use author-page citations, but it is the style of the humanities, not nursing.
whyNot.1: MLA is a humanities style, and its in-text system is author-page, not author-date.
whyNot.2: APA is the right style, but its in-text system is author-date; author-page belongs to MLA.

B.q: Original sentence (Chen, 2023): "Students who study in short daily sessions tend to remember more than students who cram the night before an exam." Which version is an acceptable paraphrase?
options: Students who study in short daily sessions remember more than those who cram (Chen, 2023).
"Students who study in short daily sessions tend to remember more" (Chen, 2023).
A little studying every day tends to beat a last-minute cram for memory (Chen, 2023).
A little studying every day tends to beat a last-minute cram for memory.
B.why: This version uses new words and a new sentence structure and still cites Chen, which is exactly what a paraphrase requires.

whyNot.0: This keeps the original wording and structure with a few cuts: patchwriting, even with a citation.
whyNot.1: This is a correctly cited direct quotation, not a paraphrase.
whyNot.3: The wording is new, but the citation is missing, so the idea is presented as the student's own.

options: Submitting last term's essay again without permission
Quoting a sentence in quotation marks with a citation
Summarizing an article in your own words with a citation
Stating a widely known, undisputed fact without a citation
B.why: Reusing your own previous work without permission is a form of plagiarism, because it presents old work as new.

whyNot.1: Exact words in quotation marks with a citation is the correct way to quote.
whyNot.2: A summary in your own words with a citation credits the source properly.
whyNot.3: Widely known, undisputed facts are common knowledge and need no citation.

B.q: What is the main difference between a paraphrase and a summary?
options: A summary uses the author's exact words and sentence order
A paraphrase is much shorter and covers the main ideas
A paraphrase needs a citation, but a summary does not
A summary is much shorter and keeps the main ideas
B.why: A paraphrase restates one passage at about the same length; a summary condenses a source to its main ideas, so it is much shorter. Both are in your own words and both are cited.

whyNot.0: Neither uses the author's exact words and order; that would be a quotation (or patchwriting).
whyNot.1: This describes a summary, not a paraphrase, which stays about the same length as the original.
whyNot.2: Both a paraphrase and a summary must be cited.

C.q: Devon copies three sentences from a website into his report, replaces several words with synonyms, keeps the original sentence order and adds a citation at the end. Which statement is accurate?
options: It is acceptable, because he cited the source
It is plagiarism, because he patchwrote the text
It is acceptable, because he changed several words
It is plagiarism, because websites are not credible
C.why: Keeping the original structure and swapping synonyms is patchwriting. A citation does not fix it: he needs quotation marks for the exact words or a true paraphrase.

whyNot.0: A citation credits the idea but does not make borrowed wording and structure his own.
whyNot.2: Synonym swaps that keep the original structure are still patchwriting.
whyNot.3: Many websites are credible sources; the problem is how he used the text, not where it came from.

C.q: When is a direct quotation the best choice for using a source?
options: When you want to avoid citing the source
When the passage is long and full of detail
When the exact wording is powerful or precise
When the idea is common knowledge among readers
C.why: Quotations should be used sparingly, for wording that is especially powerful or precise; otherwise paraphrase or summarize.

whyNot.0: A quotation always needs a citation as well as quotation marks.
whyNot.1: Long, detailed passages are usually better summarized or paraphrased than quoted at length.
whyNot.3: Common knowledge needs no source at all, so there is nothing to quote.

C.q: Brianna's APA paper has in-text citations such as (Patel, 2021) but no list of full source details. What should she add at the end of the paper?
options: A works cited page in author-page format
A reference list of all her sources
Footnotes after each paraphrased sentence
A summary of each source in the introduction
C.why: APA pairs in-text author-date citations in the body with a reference list at the end giving the full details of each source.

whyNot.0: A works cited page is the MLA name and format, not APA.
whyNot.2: The full source list goes at the end of the paper, not in footnotes after each sentence.
whyNot.3: Summaries in the introduction do not replace the list of full source details.

reteach.title: Sources are like other people's photos
reteach.question: Think about sharing a friend's photo online. How does that match quoting, paraphrasing and plagiarism?

blocks.body: Reposting a friend's photo with their tag is like a quotation: the original, plus credit. Describing the photo in your own words and still tagging them is a paraphrase. Posting a quick recap of their whole album with a tag is a summary. Posting their photo as if you took it, or tracing over it and calling it yours, is plagiarism, even if you add a filter. Only things everyone already knows need no tag.

blocks.text: A filter is not a new photo, and a few synonyms are not a new sentence. Patchwriting is plagiarism.

explain.body: The author's exact words, inside quotation marks, with a citation. Use quotations sparingly, for wording that is powerful or precise.

test.q: What is required whenever a writer uses a source's exact words?
options: A citation, without quotation marks
Quotation marks, without a citation
A footnote at the end of the page
Quotation marks and a citation
test.why: Exact words need both quotation marks (to show they are borrowed) and a citation (to show where they came from).

whyNot.0: Without quotation marks, the exact words look like the writer's own: plagiarism.
whyNot.1: Quotation marks show the words are borrowed, but the source must still be credited.
whyNot.2: A footnote alone does not mark which words are copied; quotation marks are still needed.

explain.body: A paraphrase restates one specific passage in your own words and sentence structure, at about the same length. A summary gives only the main ideas of a source, much shorter. Both are cited.

test.q: A student condenses a ten-page article into one paragraph of its main ideas, in her own words, and cites it. What has she written?
options: A summary
A paraphrase
A direct quotation
An outline
test.why: Condensing a whole source to its main ideas in your own words is a summary.

whyNot.1: A paraphrase restates one passage at about the same length, not a whole article in a paragraph.
whyNot.2: A direct quotation uses the author's exact words in quotation marks.
whyNot.3: An outline organizes the writer's own ideas during prewriting.

explain.body: Plagiarism is presenting another's words or ideas as your own: no quotation marks, patchwriting, missing citations or reusing your own work without permission. Common knowledge needs no citation.

test.q: Which is plagiarism even if the writer never copies a single sentence?
options: Quoting a source inside quotation marks and citing it
Citing a source in APA author-date style
Using another writer's idea without credit
Stating that the human heart has four chambers
test.why: Plagiarism covers ideas as well as words. Using someone's idea without crediting it presents it as your own.

whyNot.0: A quotation in quotation marks with a citation is correct use of a source.
whyNot.1: Citing in APA style credits the source properly.
whyNot.3: This is common knowledge, which needs no citation.

explain.body: APA uses author-date in-text citations, is common in nursing and the social sciences, and ends with a reference list. MLA uses author-page citations, is common in the humanities, and ends with a works cited list.

test.q: Which pairing describes a citation style's in-text system correctly?
options: APA: author-date
MLA: author-date
APA: author-title
MLA: author-title
test.why: APA cites by author and date, for example (Kim, 2024).

whyNot.1: MLA's in-text system is author-page, not author-date.
whyNot.2: APA's system is author-date; the title is not the core of its in-text citation.
whyNot.3: MLA's system is author-page; the title is not the core of its in-text citation.
